"Sharon," Kyan said, "tell the new guy he's confused." Sharon set the tomatoes on the scale and looked at James with a patience that made him feel both welcomed and slightly stupid. "This is the food bank," she said. "It's a warehouse that collects the food and sends it out to the local agencies, the pantries and the shelters and the schools. A pantry is where people actually pick up the food directly. So the guests never come here." She said it the way you'd give directions to a lost driver, quick and certain, and turned back to her scale.

James turned that over while he stacked pears. He had imagined, without ever examining the picture, a line of tired people at a counter, himself handing over a bag, some moment of contact. Instead there was this: a machine of boxes and pallets, his labor disappearing into a truck at the dock, bound for places he couldn't see. It was probably more efficient this way. He could see that. One warehouse could feed dozens of pantries instead of trying to serve a neighborhood itself. And yet the distance bothered him in a way he couldn't quite name, the sense that the good he was doing had been routed through so many intermediaries that it had become abstract, a number on a clipboard rather than a face.

At lunch, sitting on the loading dock with Sharon and Kyan and half a tomato sandwich Sharon had made from surplus, he tried to say some of this out loud. "It's like," he began, and stopped, and tried again. "You do the work here and you just have to trust it lands somewhere." Kyan shrugged. "You want the medal or the food?" He said it without cruelty, just his usual dry delivery. Sharon was more generous. "My dad used to impugn the whole system," she said. "Said the middlemen ate the budget. Then he toured the warehouse and saw the books, and now he's on the board." She laughed a little. "Turns out being suspicious is easy and being useful is boring."

James thought of his uncle, who watched videos at family dinners about how the elites ran everything, and how confident the man sounded compared to Sharon's father with his boring books. There was a kind of politics that ran on that confidence, a populist anger that felt like clarity, and next to it the actual machinery of pears and pallets looked dull, almost evasive, as if it were hiding something by being so unglamorous. But maybe it wasn't hiding anything. Maybe it was just work, and work didn't perform. He didn't know. He noticed he didn't know, and noticed that not knowing, for once, didn't make him want to pick a side immediately.

Ms. Rahman, the volunteer coordinator, came out around then with the afternoon assignments. She gave Kyan the forklift area, Sharon the garden rows, and James the dock, where a van from a church pantry was due at two. He loaded crate after crate onto a hand truck while a thin man with tired eyes counted boxes and signed a sheet, and when the last crate went up, the man said, "These pears are a big deal at my place. People ask for them by name." James watched the van pull away through the chain-link gate, then went back inside for the second pallet, box cutter already out.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A statistically significant result can still be a tiny effect: with a very large sample, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test.
story:
Jordan had told everyone, including himself, that he would have the review drafted by Friday, and it was now Sunday afternoon and he had a title, one sentence of the title, and a grandfather who kept refilling his tea without being asked. The two articles sat open on the laptop at the kitchen table: Ms. Littlechild had assigned them in the first week of term, one claiming a link between late-night phone use and poor sleep in teenagers, the other finding nothing of the kind. Jordan had picked them because they disagreed, which had seemed like an easy structure at the time. Now the disagreement looked less like a wall he could lean on and more like a hole he was expected to walk into and describe.

"Still fighting with it?" his grandfather asked, setting down the teapot with the exaggerated care of a man who wanted to be asked what he thought.

"I'm basically done," Jordan said. "It's just wording." This was not true, and some part of him knew it, the same part that had spent Saturday alphabetizing his music library.

The first article had a sample of forty thousand students, drawn from schools across three countries, and it announced, in its abstract, a statistically significant association between phone use after ten and reduced sleep. The second had four hundred students from a single town and reported no significant effect. The first article was dressed in confident language, glossy figures, a journal name Jordan recognized from the news. The second was plain, almost apologetic. He had decided, at first glance, that the first one won, and he had written his one sentence accordingly: the large study's finding was significant, the small study's was not, and that was that.

Kira had texted him twice that morning. How's the essay going, and then, ten minutes later, You've picked a side already haven't you. She knew him too well for comfort. He typed back a denial, deleted it, and typed Have you looked at the numbers though, and she replied with a single question mark, which in Kira's language meant come over or call me, I'm not doing this by text. He called her from the back step, where the garden ran down to a hedge and a greenhouse with one cracked pane his grandfather kept meaning to fix.

"The big study says significant," Jordan said, before she could speak. "So it's real."

"Significant," Kira repeated, in the flat tone she used when she thought he was coasting. "Do you know what the difference actually was? Like, how big?"

He didn't. He had not thought there was a difference between real and big; the word significant had underpinned the whole first draft, and he had let it carry weight it maybe didn't have. He went back inside, past his grandfather, who was pretending to read the paper and clearly listening, and found the table in the first article, the one he had skimmed because tables felt like homework inside homework. The numbers were there. The sleep difference between heavy phone users and light ones was small. Genuinely small. A matter of minutes.

He sat with that for a while. Forty thousand students, and the gap the study had trumpeted was a sliver of an hour. He remembered Ms. Littlechild saying something in class about how, with a very large sample, even a difference too small to matter in practice can pass the significance test, and he had written it down without understanding it, the way you write down things you assume will matter later. Later had arrived. The second study, the one he had dismissed, had four hundred students and could probably only have detected a large effect, and it hadn't found one, which now seemed less like a failure and more like a piece of information. The two articles weren't simply opposed. They were answering slightly different questions, or answering the same question with instruments of different fineness, like trying to measure a fjord with a ruler and then with a satellite: the satellite would find the fjord, but it would not tell you how cold the water was.

His grandfather came over and read the abstract on the screen, slowly, moving his lips. "Significant," he said. "That means it matters."

"That's what I thought," Jordan said. "It doesn't, exactly. It means it's probably not nothing. It can be probably not nothing and still be too small to care about."

His grandfather looked at him for a long moment. "Your grandmother reviewed papers, you know. Before her knees went. She used to say the worst reviews only tell you whether the author was right. The good ones tell you what the author was right about." He went back to his chair, leaving Jordan with that, and with the strange sensation of a sentence rearranging itself behind his eyes.

He opened a new document and began again. He wrote that the first study was probably correct about the direction of its finding and that its size made even a minute difference register as significant; he wrote that the second study, though limited, found nothing that rose above noise, and that the honest reading was somewhere between the two articles rather than inside either. He wrote that he could not say how big the effect would be for any particular student, because neither article could say that either, and that the question of what mattered in practice was not one the statistics answered by themselves. It was the most uncertain thing he had ever put in an essay on purpose. It felt like standing on a floor that moved slightly, and choosing to stand on it anyway.

Kira texted again at dusk: So did you pick a side. He looked at the draft, at the small hours of sleep on the table, at his grandfather asleep in the chair with the paper sliding off his knee. Kind of, he typed. A side with a gap in it. Then he closed the laptop, carried the paper to the recycling, and put the teapot away.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Chemist Michel Eugène Chevreul published his law of simultaneous contrast in 1839, describing how a color appears to shift toward the complement of the color placed next to it.
story:
Kaitlyn had mixed the gray herself, on a paper plate in the art shed at Camp Wren, stirring black into white with a broken popsicle stick until the two colors gave up their separate names. She was painting the rocks along the lake shore for the Friday night show, four days away, and the rocks had to be gray because the rocks were gray. But when she laid the paint down beside a patch of teal water, the same gray went lavender and cool. Two inches over, next to a band of burnt orange she had used for the canoe hull, it turned smoky and warm, almost taupe. She dipped her stick back into the plate, touched the plate itself, and confirmed what she already suspected: the paint was one gray, uniform, indifferent. The difference was happening somewhere between the paint and her eye, and she could not stop looking at it.

Josh came in carrying a fistful of willow branches for the basket weavers and stopped behind her shoulder. "Your rocks are two different colors," he said.

"They're one color," Kaitlyn said. "That's the problem."

He leaned closer, close enough that she could smell the lake on him, and squinted. "Looks like two to me. Is that on purpose?"

"I don't know yet." She said it honestly, because around Josh she usually did. "If it's on purpose, it's good. If it's an accident, it's a mistake. Same painting either way."

Mr. Silva-Jayasuriya, who ran the art shed and also, inexplicably, the astronomy hour, was out by the dock repairing a kiln shelf. Kaitlyn carried the canvas to the window and held it in the light. The lake itself lay flat and bright beyond the screen, the real rocks along its edge doing whatever real rocks did when nobody painted them. She wondered whether her eye was wrong or her paint was wrong, and which of those she was supposed to fix by Friday.

Laila found her at lunch with the canvas propped against the picnic table, shielded from the wind with a rock on each corner. Laila was the only person at camp who had brought a library book, a fat orange paperback about color, and she had been reading it all week in the hammock, announcing fragments aloud to no one. She set her tray down and looked at the painting for a long time before she spoke.

"Each color looks different depending on what's next to it," Laila said. "It pulls toward the opposite of the neighboring one. So your gray goes warm next to the teal and cool next to the orange." She flipped pages with one thumb. "Here. A chemist figured this out. Michel Eugène Chevreul. He published it in 1839. It's called the law of simultaneous contrast."

"Simultaneous contrast," Kaitlyn repeated, tasting it. "So the paint didn't change. The neighbors did it."

From Josh's view, across the table, the exchange looked like a negotiation between two people who each wanted to be right but were too tired to argue properly. He watched Kaitlyn hold the book at arm's length, then close to her face, then hand it back. He watched Laila point at the teal and say something he couldn't hear over the wind. What he noticed, and what he doubted either of them had noticed, was that Kaitlyn had stopped defending the painting. All summer she had answered every comment about her work like a small claim being impugned, as if anyone who questioned a brushstroke were questioning her. Now she was asking questions back, and something in her shoulders had come down an inch.

After lunch she went back to the shed alone. The deadline sat in her mind the way the show schedule sat on the corkboard: check-in at five on Friday, no exceptions, and Mrs. Halloran had already made it clear that the art shed had a fiduciary duty, her words, to the camp's budget for the mat board, which meant no wasted sheets, which meant Kaitlyn had one canvas and three afternoons. She turned the painting toward the wall and worked on the smaller studies instead, gray swatches on scrap paper, each one flanked by different colors, teal and orange and a raw pink she mixed from what was left. She made a row of them like a test and taped it to the window.

The studies told her the gray would behave, that she could aim it, but they did not tell her whether she should. That was the part she turned over while rinsing her brushes in the bucket. Her mother painted photographs, exact and patient, and would have corrected the rocks until they matched. Her grandmother quilted, and once told Kaitlyn that a quilt lies on purpose, that you choose the lie that pleases. Two different inheritances, and the painting wanted an answer by Friday. She decided, provisionally, to trust both: she would let the gray shift, but she would shift it knowingly, mixing one gray for the teal side and another for the orange side, so the rocks would differ the way the lake made them differ. Whether that was a solution or a sophisticated surrender she could not yet say, and she let the uncertainty stand, the way the metamorphic rocks along the shore had stood through whatever pressures had made them, changed but still themselves.

On Friday afternoon she carried the canvas to the check-in table, the lake behind her going gold at the edges, and set it down in front of the clipboard. The volunteer looked at it, then at her, and said, "Title?"

Kaitlyn looked at the two grays, warm and cool, one paint beside the water and one beside the hull. "One Gray," she said. "Two."

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: Canada's federal Goods and Services Tax, introduced on January 1, 1991 at 7 percent, has been 5 percent since January 1, 2008.
story:
I found the receipt in my jacket pocket on the morning of the tax appointment, folded into a square the size of a stamp. It was from the hardware store where I'd bought paint for the set of the school play, nineteen dollars and change with a line underneath that said GST, ninety-five cents. Ninety-five cents was five percent of nineteen dollars. I stood in the kitchen doing that math twice, because the last time I'd checked a receipt, at my part-time job at the party supply store, I had told a customer the GST was seven percent and she had looked at me the way you look at a cashier who has just invented a number.

"Alexis, we're going to be late," my father called from the hall. He believed that arriving early to an accountant's office was a virtue and arriving on time was a character flaw.

Mr. Adeyemi's office was on the second floor above a florist, a room of grey filing cabinets and a ficus that had given up on something. My father spread his papers across the desk the way other men spread maps. I sat by the window with my own small stack: my T4 slip, my pay stubs, my bank statement. I had been working Saturdays and two evenings a week since September, and I wanted my refund. I had done a rough calculation on my phone in the dark the night before and arrived at a figure that would cover half of a used laptop for college. The laptop was the whole point. Margot had one and Pyper had one and I had been borrowing the library's machines like a person borrowing umbrellas, always returning them slightly damp.

Mr. Adeyemi went through my father's return first, unhurried, tapping keys. Words drifted across the desk that I had seen before only as abbreviations on my stub: income tax, CPP, EI. Deductions, he said, meaning the difference between what I earned and what arrived in my account every other Thursday. I had noticed the gap months ago and had been quietly sullen about it, in the way of someone who suspects the universe of taking a cut. Now the abbreviations turned out to be things with names and rules, and the rules were printed on paper I could read.

While my father and Mr. Adeyemi talked about RRSPs, I texted Margot, who worked at the shoe store in the mall and checked receipts all day.

"Is GST five or seven?" I typed.

"Five," she wrote back, fast, as though I had asked if water was wet. "It started January 1, 1991 at seven percent, but it's been five percent since January 1, 2008. Somebody asked me yesterday too."

So I had told that customer the rate from before I was born. I had been confident about it, which was the embarrassing part. I would have to go back to the party supply store and hope she never returned, or hope she did, so I could disabuse her of the number I had planted. I wrote 5% in the margin of my pay stub, next to a lemma I'd copied out for calculus homework, since the appointment was eating my study evening. A lemma, my textbook insisted, was a small proved thing you used to prove a bigger thing. It occurred to me that the receipt in my pocket was something like that: a small fact that made a larger one visible.

Then Mr. Adeyemi turned to my stack, and I stopped philosophizing, because the number on his screen was not the number from my dark-room calculation.

From the doorway, if anyone had been standing there, they would have seen a girl lean forward so fast her chair legs barked against the floor. Mr. Adeyemi rotated the monitor toward her with two fingers, patient, the way a man rotates a chessboard he has already won.

"That's less," Alexis said. "That's almost forty dollars less than I worked out."

"You estimated your tax payable at zero," he said. "You're under the basic personal amount, so most of what was withheld comes back. Most." He tapped a line. "But not the CPP, and there's a small provincial piece. The refund is what's left over."

Alexis looked at the screen. The figure sat there, solid and indifferent, roughly two-thirds of a used laptop. Behind her, her father was saying something about contributions, and the words went past her like traffic.

"Could I," she began, and stopped. She had been ready to argue, the way she argued with Pyper about whose turn it was to buy the coffee, but there was nothing to argue with. The number wasn't an opinion. It was arithmetic, done by a man who did arithmetic for a living, and she had simply left a piece out.

She thought of her father, who filed every spring with his shoebox of receipts, and of Margot, who knew the sales tax the way Alexis knew the periodic table. There was something to be said for knowing the actual rules instead of the vibes of the rules. And yet the rules weren't secret; they were printed on the stub she had stuffed, unread, into a drawer for eight months. Both things were true at once, and she held them together without deciding which one to be more embarrassed about.

Mr. Adeyemi printed the return. "Sign here, and here. Refund by direct deposit, probably two weeks."

"Two weeks," Alexis said. She signed, and the pen skipped on the second line, and she did it again.

Outside, the florist was hosing down the sidewalk. Alexis took the hardware store receipt out of her pocket, unfolded it, and held it up to the light as though it might have changed. Ninety-five cents. Five percent. She put it back, carefully, in the pocket with her calculator homework.

"Next Saturday I'm picking up extra shifts," she said. "And I'm asking for one of the register-training days."

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: The FAFSA is the form US students complete to apply for federal financial aid such as Pell Grants and federal loans, and many states and colleges also use it to award their own aid.
story:
The folder in Naomi's lap held everything Mr. Adeyemi had asked for, and one thing he hadn't: the rejection letter from Carver, which she had told no one about, not even Alycia, who had been reciting her own acceptances in the cafeteria like a rosary. She had decided on the walk over that the letter was not a rejection exactly. It was a deferral. Those were different words the way "thrifty" and "cheap" were different words, and she was aware that the distinction mostly existed to make her feel better, which did not stop her from making it.

"You're quiet today," Mr. Adeyemi said. He was not a choleric man; she had never once heard him raise his voice, even when Devon set off the fire alarm with a bagel. His office smelled like pencil shavings and the fake lemon of his desk spray. He slid his chair back and waited, which was his whole method, she was pretty sure: wait long enough and a kid would say anything.

"Meritwick said my file was complete," she said. "In October. Then last week they said it wasn't, because the aid form never came in."

"FAFSA?"

"My mom did it." She heard the defensiveness in her own voice and flattened it. "We did it together, actually, in the kitchen, on her laptop, at like eleven at night, because the state deadline was the next day. She kept saying she understood it and I kept not believing her, and then it turned out she did understand it better than me. It's the form for federal money, the Pell Grant, the loans, that kind of thing. But it's not just federal. The state uses it for its own aid too, and a lot of colleges use it for theirs. So if it's late or wrong, you're not just late for one thing. You're late for everything." She hadn't known that in October. In October she had thought of it as one errand among many, a box to check, and she had let her mother carry most of it while she wrote her essay about carrying things.

"What went wrong?"

"Nothing went wrong. That's the thing. We checked last night and it went through on the deadline. But Meritwick's portal still says missing, and their aid office closes at four, and the woman on the phone said to wait ten business days, and ten business days is after their aid priority date, which I only know because Alycia read it out loud from her letter while I was standing there holding my own letter which does not say that because my letter assumes I already know things."

Mr. Adeyemi wrote a number on a sticky note and passed it across. "Direct line, not the main one. Ask for the processing unit, not admissions." He leaned back. "You said you didn't tell anyone about Carver."

She stared at him, then at the folder, where the letter was, fifth page back, because she had put it there herself, and he had watched her do it, or noticed the thickness, or simply knew that everyone in March was carrying one. "I didn't say that."

"You organized the pages in a specific order when you sat down. Transcript, resume, Meritwick correspondence. Then a page you turned face down. I've done this job a while."

She wanted to call this a trick, and for a moment she did, silently, the way she called the deferral a deferral. But he wasn't performing insight; he was just paying attention, which was rarer and less theatrical than she'd credited. Her mother, at the kitchen table at eleven, had said something similar in her own way. Naomi had been trying to parametrize the whole application, her mother had said, like it was a function where you control the inputs and get the output you earned. "Life is not math, baby," she'd said, and Naomi had privately disagreed, and privately agreed, and not resolved it.

"It's a deferral," Naomi said now, out loud, testing it.

"Which you'll answer how?"

"Send grades from this term. The calculus grade. Naila thinks I should also send the thing about the debate tournament, but that feels like begging." She paused. "Naila said a worse thing, actually. She said Meritwick only defers people they want to reject politely. She has a whole theory that every nice word in these letters is a dysphemism, that 'we were impressed by' means 'we skimmed,' that 'space is limited' means 'go away.' She's probably wrong. She's wrong about a lot. But she might not be wrong."

Mr. Adeyemi turned the sticky note around so the number faced her. "Call Meritwick first," he said. "Then decide what Carver means, or what you'll make it mean. Those are two different tasks, and only one of them has a deadline."

She took the note. Out the window behind him, the parking lot was half empty and a maintenance guy was chalking a line along the curb for no reason she could determine, steady and unhurried, the chalk dust lifting a little in the wind.

She folded the note into her pocket and stood, and picked up the folder, and left the face-down page where it was.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Consent to sexual activity must be freely given and can be withdrawn at any time, including after activity has already started.
story:
The pharmacy sat between a nail salon and a shuttered video store, and on Tuesday afternoons it was Sofia's post. She had joined the peer health program in September mostly because Ms. Müller, the pharmacist, had agreed to let students use the counter as a practice site, and because Sofia needed something on her application that sounded like initiative. The deal was simple: Sofia shadowed Ms. Müller, learned where the contraception was stocked, memorized the walk-in clinic's hours, and answered questions from classmates when they came in, which they did more often than she had expected.

That Tuesday, Alex came in at four, wearing the grey hoodie from cross-country, and stood in the aisle of condoms for six minutes without touching anything. Sofia watched from behind the register, where she was helping an older woman transliterate the dosage on a prescription label into Cyrillic so the woman's mother could sound it out in her own alphabet. When the woman left, Sofia walked over to Alex.

"I have to buy them for a health thing," Alex said. "For the class. Ms. Müller knows."

"She doesn't, but okay." Sofia took two boxes down and compared them, then pointed at the shelf above. "The clinic gives them out free, by the way. You just ask at the front desk. You don't even need a reason." She said it the way she'd practiced saying it, level, no eyebrow raised, the way Ms. Müller said things about lactic acid and generic brands.

Alex put the box on the counter, then didn't take out a wallet. "Can I ask you the thing people ask you? The thing you're supposed to know now." Sofia nodded. There was a rack of pamphlets beside the register, fanned out like an archipelago, chlamydia on one island, the pill on another, and Alex glanced at them as if the answer might be printed there. "If someone says yes. At the start. Does that mean it's a yes the whole way through? Like, it's already happening, so." Alex swallowed. "For a friend."

"No," Sofia said, and heard the word come out steadier than she felt. "It has to be freely given, and you can take it back at any time. Even after it's started." She had read the sentence in the training binder weeks ago and had underlined it twice, partly because it seemed too simple to need underlining and partly because she had once believed the opposite and had never corrected herself out loud until the role-play in health class, when a boy playing the doctor had asked the same question and she had frozen, and Ms. Müller, watching from the back, had said nothing at all, which had been its own kind of answer.

"Even in the middle of it," Alex said.

"Even in the middle of it. Freely given, and it can be withdrawn whenever." Sofia slid the box across the counter and rang it up, because standing still with that sentence between them was harder than pressing buttons. "And if the friend wants to get tested, the clinic does it walk-in on Thursdays. They swab or they take urine, depending. Results in about a week. Nobody calls your house."

Alex paid, in coins, mostly quarters. Then Alex took the pamphlet on contraception, the one Sofia always pushed because it had the copper IUD diagram with the little copper wire, drawn fine and bent, the way copper actually was, ductile enough to wrap and hold its shape, which Sofia had found oddly reassuring. Alex folded the pamphlet into eighths and put it in the pocket with the quarters.

They stood there a moment in the fluorescent quiet. Behind them Ms. Müller was counting trays of pills, not looking over, and Sofia understood that she had not looked over once, that the whole exchange had been left to run on its own.

"It wasn't for a friend," Alex said, zipping the hoodie to the chin. "And it wasn't about me changing my mind. It was about whether I could tell someone else they were allowed to." Then Alex picked up the bag and left, the door chime going off behind them, and Sofia turned back to the register and found, lying on the counter where the coins had been, the clinic appointment card with her own name on it, dropped there sometime during the transaction, Thursday, four-thirty, circled twice.

activity: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
knowledge_domain: the language of contracts and forms, such as terms, conditions, liability, consent and signatures
fact: In common-law countries such as the US, UK and Canada, a contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side in exchange.
story:
The phone store smelled of floor cleaner and warm plastic, and Samantha stood at the counter holding her mother's old flip phone like an artifact from an ascetic age, a device that did nothing but call and text and survive being dropped. She had saved for eleven weeks. Tonight she wanted a phone of her own, in her own name, with a plan she paid for herself, because in September she would be three hundred miles from home and tired of borrowing.

Mr. Ma, who owned the store and had sold her mother a car charger once, slid a form across the counter and clicked a pen twice against the glass. "This is the agreement for the plan," he said. "Terms on the front, conditions on the back. Take your time."

She took her time. The print was small and the clauses marched on, early termination fees, liability for damage, consent to credit checks, and near the bottom a line of empty boxes for initials, one for every section, as if the paper wanted her to agree twelve separate times before she agreed once. Behind her, Noa wandered the display wall, picking up demo phones and setting them down in the wrong spots.

Samantha's problem was not the fine print, though. Her problem was that the deposit took almost everything she had, and she had been counting on two hundred dollars from Maxim. He had texted her three weeks ago, I'll pay you $200 if you get me through the calc final, and she had said deal, and she had gotten him through it, four Sunday afternoons at the library with his graphing calculator and her patience. Since the final he had gone quiet in a way that seemed to presage exactly this, the long gaps between replies, the answers that weren't answers, until yesterday he wrote can we talk about the money thing.

She had answered sure and he had left her on read. Now the deposit box on Mr. Ma's screen waited at $150, and her checking account held $168.

"So I sign here," she said, "and the phone is mine."

"You sign, and the contract is formed," Mr. Ma said. "A contract generally needs an offer, an acceptance, and consideration, meaning something of value given by each side. Here they offer you the service, you accept, and you pay the monthly fee. That's your consideration."

Noa drifted over and leaned on the counter. "Maxim still owes you, right? That's a contract too. He offered, you accepted."

"He offered two hundred, I said deal." Samantha turned the pen over in her fingers. "But the consideration part is what I keep worrying about. What I gave him was already given. The tutoring's finished. Sitting here with the money still owed feels different from signing this." She looked at the initial boxes, twelve small surrenders. If she signed and Maxim never paid, the shortfall would be hers alone, and a missed payment, the form warned in a clause about reporting to credit bureaus, could be deleterious to her credit for years. She was eighteen. Her credit was a clean, empty page.

The bell over the door rang. Maxim came in with his jacket still on, looking at the carpet, and stopped two feet from the counter as though the floor had turned slippery. "I got your message," he said. "I came because you're here."

"Convenient," Samantha said.

"I can pay you eighty now and the rest when my paycheck comes." He pulled a folded wad of bills from his pocket, and his hand stayed closed around it. "My mom's hours got cut. I should have told you that part first."

The store hummed. Noa picked up a demo phone and pretended to examine it. Mr. Ma looked at his screen with the courtesy of a man watching nothing.

Samantha thought about the form in front of her, offer and acceptance, value moving both ways, and about the four Sundays in the library, which had felt like friendship right up until they felt like an invoice. She had been ready to argue the whole thing was binding, to stand on the texting records like a lawyer in a commercial. Now she was not sure which she wanted less, the two hundred dollars or the reason she'd stopped expecting them.

"Pay me the eighty," she said. "Not here. Come outside, because I'm about to be in a contract with a phone company and I don't want to think about yours at the same time." She slid the form back toward Mr. Ma. "Can I initial everything and pay the deposit in cash? Part of it's coming in a minute."

Mr. Ma clicked his pen once and held it out to her, and through the window she watched Maxim counting the bills into Noa's hand for safekeeping, folding each one in half first, like something he was reluctant to let go of.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about 95 degrees Celsius at 5,000 feet, so boiled foods take longer to cook.
story:
Nicolas had promised his mother a real dinner, cooked by him alone, before the family drove up to the cabin for the weekend, and the farmers' market on Saturday morning was where he intended to make it happen. He carried a canvas bag and a list written on the back of a subpoena that had come addressed to the previous tenant of their apartment, a man named Gerald who apparently owed somebody money and a great deal of it. The paper had a certain official weight that Nicolas enjoyed. It made grocery lists feel binding.

At the tomato stall he ran into Koby, who was buying peppers with the seriousness of a man purchasing a car. "You're still doing the dinner thing," Koby said. "I thought you'd bail." Nicolas held up the subpoena-list as evidence of his commitment. "This is legally enforceable now," he said, and Koby laughed so hard a pepper nearly escaped his hand.

The problem revealed itself gradually. Nicolas had planned pasta with market vegetables, a dish he had made a dozen times at home, where it took eleven minutes and came out perfect. But the cabin, as his mother reminded him by text, sat at five thousand feet, and Nicolas had never cooked there. He was turning this over at Mr. Nkosi's stall, where the old man sold honey and eggs and, inexplicably, a single small shelf of dry pasta, when Rayne appeared beside him holding a jar of something purple.

"You're frowning at noodles," Rayne said. "That's a new level of Nicolas." He explained the situation: the dinner, the altitude, the eleven minutes. Rayne, who had spent last summer at her uncle's place in the mountains, picked up a bag of pasta and examined it as if it might confess something. "Water boils at a lower temperature at high altitude, about ninety-five degrees Celsius at five thousand feet," she said, "so boiled foods take longer to cook." Then she added, with great satisfaction, "Your pasta's going to be crunchy, Nicolas. Crunchy like a moral failing."

"So I just boil it longer," Nicolas said, and immediately heard how little he liked the plan. Longer was vague. Longer could mean gummy. He wanted a rule, a number, something as certain as the eleven minutes written in his mother's margin of the recipe. Rayne shrugged. "Or you could make something that doesn't care about altitude. Roast the vegetables, do it in the oven, bread on the side." Koby, arriving with his peppers, was effusive in his agreement: oven food, oven food, oven food, a small chant. Nicolas pointed out that the whole point of the dinner had been the pasta, which his father called the only dish Nicolas made that he would cross a street for.

Mr. Nkosi, who had been listening while weighing honey, did not offer wisdom. He only said, "Some people up there cook rice for hours," and went back to his scale, which was the most useful thing anyone had said all morning, because it confirmed that the problem was real and that Nicolas had not been defeated by his own imagination.

He walked the market twice with the two plans arguing in his head. The oven dinner was safer; it would taste good; his father would eat it politely and say nothing about pasta. The pasta was a gamble on longer, an amount of time he would have to guess, standing at a stove at five thousand feet while his family waited and got hungrier and kinder in the way of hungry people trying not to say so. He bought the vegetables for roasting anyway, because Rayne was right about the vegetables. Then he stood in front of Mr. Nkosi's little pasta shelf for a long moment, and bought a bag of that too.

At the cabin that evening, the water rolled to its strangely gentle boil, and Nicolas set a timer for eleven minutes and then, when the pasta came up hard and pale in the middle, kept going, testing a piece every minute like a man defusing something. Nineteen minutes. His father, waiting at the table, said, "Is this a hostage situation?" and Nicolas said, "Yes, and you're under subpoena," waving the official paper, and his mother laughed in a way that made the extra eight minutes feel like they had been worth it, though the pasta was, in truth, only mostly done, one strand of it still faintly stubborn in the center, and Nicolas ate that one himself without telling anyone.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: A launch velocity v at an angle θ above the horizontal splits into a horizontal component v cos θ and a vertical component v sin θ.
story:
Felix had promised himself he would not spend his last summer before college standing in front of the projectile table at the science museum for a third consecutive afternoon, and yet there he was, feeding tokens into the launcher while Ahmed leaned against the rail eating fries he had smuggled in from the food court.

The table was simple to the point of insult. An air cannon, a protractor printed on the housing, a target ring bolted into the turf fifteen meters out, and a readout that told you the launch velocity and nothing else. The trick, which the museum placard announced in cheerful orange letters, was that you had to tell the machine the angle yourself, and it would fire wherever you aimed. Felix had missed the ring eleven times.

"You're overthinking it," Ahmed said, mouth full. "Just aim at the target. Like a basketball."

"It's not like a basketball. The velocity is fixed. The angle is the only thing I control." Felix set the dial to sixty degrees and fired. The ball climbed, hung, and dropped a full two meters short of the ring. Ahmed said nothing, which in Ahmed's language was a eulogy.

Reda arrived twenty minutes late the next day, which was early for her, carrying a notebook she had already filled with diagrams. She had taken physics the year before Felix did, and she had opinions about why he was failing. "You keep treating the diagonal like it's one thing," she said, tapping the placard. "It's not one thing. A velocity at an angle splits. Horizontal part, vertical part. They don't talk to each other."

Felix looked at the placard, which said exactly that in smaller, less confident letters than the orange announcement. "Fine. Split into what?"

"Into sine and cosine of the angle." She drew a slanted arrow, dropped a vertical line from its tip, closed the rectangle. "Horizontal component is v cosine theta. Vertical is v sine theta." She said it the way she recited locker combinations, bored and precise.

On Thursday Mr. Halvorsen, the retired engineer who volunteered at the museum on weekdays and repaired the launcher whenever a bearing went, watched Felix punch numbers into his calculator and shake his head. Felix had decided the vertical component was v cosine theta and the horizontal was v sine theta, and he had aimed accordingly, low and flat, certain that a nearly level launch would send the ball climbing steeply. It did not. It skimmed the turf like a stone across a pond and cracked against the barrier six meters out.

"You look like a man arguing with a parking meter," Mr. Halvorsen said. He did not offer the answer. He had a stoicism about hints that Felix found, in that moment, intransigent and faintly cruel, though later he would recognize it as courtesy.

Felix sat on the floor of the mezzanine with Reda's notebook and tried it both ways. If the vertical component were cosine, then a launch angled almost flat, near zero degrees, would have a vertical component near the full velocity, near the whole arrow, which would mean a ball launched almost horizontally would fly almost straight up. He fired a token at five degrees and watched the ball travel in a long, shallow, unmistakable arc. It did not go up. Nothing about it augured vertical grandeur. The horizontal component, then, must be cosine, standing almost whole when the angle was small, and the vertical must be sine, shrinking toward nothing as the launch flattened. He checked Reda's sentence against the five-degree flight and then against the sixty-degree shot from Tuesday, the one that had climbed so high and fallen so short, and the two failures agreed with each other for the first time all week.

He chose thirty-five degrees. Ahmed abandoned his fries to watch. Reda held the notebook against her chest like a hymnal. The ball rose, drifted, and dropped through the ring with a plastic clatter that sounded, to Felix, unreasonably loud.

The readout reset. Fifteen meters, fixed velocity, and an empty space where the target could be moved by whoever ran the exhibit next, and Felix realized he did not know whether thirty-five degrees was the answer or merely an answer, whether some other angle might also have landed, whether the whole business had one solution or a family of them. He fed in another token and turned the dial slowly, watching the number change.

"Same angle?" Ahmed asked.

"Close," Felix said. "Let's see what thirty-four does."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
The first loaf came out of the oven looking like a doorstop, and Ryan cut into it while it was still warm because he couldn't wait. The crumb was dense and crumbly, closer to a biscuit than to bread, and it fell apart in his hands when he tried to butter a slice. His father ate a piece anyway and said it was fine, but Ryan could tell from the careful way he chewed that fine was a veneer over something less generous.

He had followed the recipe. He had measured the flour level with the back of a knife, warmed the water to the temperature the recipe wanted, waited the full hour for the dough to rise. The dough had never felt right under his palms, though, and when he'd tried to stretch it, it tore instead of stretching thin. He had kneaded it for maybe four minutes, until his arms got tired and the kitchen timer seemed like enough of an excuse to stop.

His mother had started a new schedule at the hospital, which was why he was cooking at all, and tonight was his second attempt. He set the flour and the yeast and the salt on the counter in a row and turned on his phone, propping it against the sugar canister. Blair had texted him a link that morning with no comment except "read the whole thing," and he read the whole thing.

There it was. Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier. He read the sentence twice. He had given the dough water and he had given it almost no time. Four minutes of half-hearted pushing had left the proteins mixed but the network barely built, and a weak network meant a loaf that couldn't hold the gas the yeast made, which meant dense, which meant crumbly, which meant the doorstop cooling on the bread board as evidence.

Alexus came over at four, partly to help and partly because she said she refused to believe he was doing this voluntarily. She leaned against the fridge and watched him mix the dough, and when he told her about the glutenin and the gliadin she repeated the words back to him slowly, like she was testing whether they were real.

"Say that again," she said.

"Glutenin and gliadin. They're the wheat proteins. They mix with the water and that's when gluten forms." He dusted the counter with flour and turned the shaggy mass out onto it. "Kneading longer makes the network stronger, and the bread chewier. I stopped way too early last time."

"So how long is long enough?"

He didn't know, exactly. The recipe said eight to ten minutes. The article said the windowpane test, which meant stretching a piece of dough until light passed through it without tearing, and he liked that better than a number because the number felt like it belonged to someone else's flour, someone else's hands. He told Alexus this and she said that was the most prevaricating answer to a simple question she'd ever heard, and he said it wasn't prevaricating if he actually didn't know, and she said that was exactly what someone prevaricating would say, and then he started kneading so he wouldn't have to win.

The dough changed under his hands. For the first five minutes it stuck and tore and generally behaved like something that wanted nothing to do with him. Then, somewhere around the seventh minute, it began to smooth out, to come together into a single surface that pushed back when he pushed. He broke off a piece and stretched it. It tore. He kept going, folding and pressing, turning the dough a quarter turn each time the way the video had shown, and at what his phone said was eleven minutes he broke off another piece and pulled it gently outward, and this time it thinned and thinned until he could see the window through it, a pale gray blur of afternoon light through the dough.

Mr. Bakker from next door knocked on the back door while the dough was rising, holding a plate he wanted returned, and stood in the doorway with his usual saturnine expression while Ryan explained what was in the bowl. He said his own mother had made bread every Saturday and never once called anything a windowpane, and Ryan said he didn't think she'd needed to, and Mr. Bakker almost smiled, which for him was practically applause.

The second loaf browned evenly and sounded hollow when Ryan knocked the bottom of the pan, which the recipe said it should. He turned it out onto the rack and stood there while it cooled, with Alexus on a stool beside him and his father due home in twenty minutes and his mother due home at eleven. There was a chance the crumb would still be wrong, some other variable he hadn't learned yet, the flour or the weather or something with no name he knew. But when he cut the first slice, the knife met almost no resistance, and the inside opened in irregular holes, and steam rose off it into the kitchen light.

Alexus took the piece he held out, and buttered it, and ate it standing up.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passes with no more than 15 driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults.
story:
Carter had the school parking lot to himself for exactly forty minutes, because at four o'clock the janitor chained the gate and Mr. Fitzgerald, who taught geography and lived two streets over, liked to walk home through it. He set up two recycling bins with a jump rope stretched between them and backed his mother's recalcitrant hatchback toward the gap, easing off the clutch until the car shuddered and stalled.

"Tomorrow, right?" Aleeza was sitting on the low wall by the science wing, hood up, eating crisps from a bag she held out to him without looking. "Because I need you to pass. Saturday. The coach depot at nine, and the trains are on strike, and I am not carrying my cello on two buses."

"I know." He restarted the engine. "You've said."

"Twice only." She came over and stood where he could see her in the wing mirror, arms crossed, unofficial examiner. He reversed until the tyres kissed the curb, a soft but definite kiss, and stopped with his forehead on the wheel.

"That's the third time," she said.

In Britain the test was scored by faults, and the rules were printed in the booklet his mother had ordered online, which he had read twice in bed and once more at lunch. A candidate passed with no more than fifteen driving faults, and with no serious or dangerous faults at all. The words had sat oddly with him all day. Fifteen sounded generous until you understood the other half, that one serious fault ended you, and he had spent sixth form learning to ascribe every bad outcome to some fixed trait in himself, an inability, a deficit, so that a single clipped curb could feel like a verdict rather than an event. The booklet suggested something else: that mistakes came in kinds, and only some kinds were fatal, and the apportionment between them was the whole business.

He pulled forward and tried again. This time he brought the wheel around earlier, watched the bin in the left mirror slide toward the car's flank, and straightened out with a hand's width of clearance. He sat there. It was not elegant, but nothing had touched anything.

"Better," Aleeza said, in the tone of someone grading generously and knowing it.

"Listen," he said. "If I touch the curb once tomorrow, that's a driving fault. It counts against me, but it doesn't fail me on its own. I could have up to fifteen. What fails you is a serious fault or a dangerous one. Touching the curb isn't either." He had wanted to say it aloud to hear whether he believed it.

"So touch it fourteen more times, basically."

"That's not what I'm saying."

"It's a bit what you're saying." She was smiling, though. She dropped into the passenger seat and pointed at the road beyond the gate. "Now the other thing. The merge. You stall on the slip road and I miss my orchestra thing and Mr. Fitzgerald has to hear me play Mahler without a second cello, and he will ascribe that to you also."

The dual carriageway past the retail park had a short slip road and a lumpy camber that his mother blamed for everything. He indicated early, checked the mirror twice because checking once felt like luck, and pressed the accelerator down as the strip of paint narrowed. A white van was in the left lane and Carter held his speed, then eased into the gap behind it without braking, and the engine note climbed and settled, and Aleeza put her crisps away, which he chose to take as respect.

They did it four more times, and on the fourth a car flashed its lights to let him in, which felt like the road itself being kind. On the way back through town he parallel parked between a postbox and somebody's trailer, first attempt, and sat with the handbrake on while a woman waited to cross.

"You're going to pass," Aleeza said.

"Maybe. The examiner might see something I don't. I might touch the curb once and spend the rest of the test waiting for the fail that isn't coming, and drive badly because of that." That was the part he could not settle: whether to treat each fault as nothing, or as the beginning of a count, and no booklet told you how to hold both in your head at once. He turned the wheel and pulled out. "Anyway. Saturday. Nine o'clock. You, me, the cello."

"Nine o'clock," she said, and reached over and straightened his mirror, which had gone crooked somewhere on the dual carriageway, and left her hand on the dash as they pulled up outside the school again, where Mr. Fitzgerald was walking home through the chained gate, coat over his arm, raising one hand to them without stopping.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: In C major the dominant seventh chord is G7, made of the notes G, B, D and F, and it pulls strongly toward the C major chord.
story:
The concert hall was empty except for the grand piano on stage and three folding chairs near the front row. Logan sat at the piano with his staff paper on the music stand, and Raina sat beside him with her own copy of his sixteen bars, marking problems in pencil. Above them the acoustic panels hung like grey sails, and somewhere at the back a janitor's cart squeaked and stopped.

He had been at the melody for two weeks. Ms. Popal had given the assignment to the whole theory class: sixteen bars, chord changes, standard notation, played for her at the end of the month in this hall, because the school rented it Fridays after five and she believed music should be learned where it would eventually be heard. His melody was fine, he thought. The ending was the problem. Bar fifteen sat on a G chord and bar sixteen landed on C, and every time he played it, the landing felt like stepping off a curb he hadn't noticed.

"It's not wrong," Raina said. "It's just nothing." She was not a sycophant; she had told him the opening was good in the same flat voice she now used for the ending, so he trusted both verdicts equally. She played his last four bars, and they sounded exactly like a sentence that stops because the speaker ran out of breath.

"That's the thing," Logan said. "Mylie's ending works and mine doesn't, and we're both going to C." Mylie had finished early, and her last two bars closed like a door. He had asked her how, and she had been vague about it, which might have been secrecy or might have been genuine uncertainty; her answer had been equivocal, something about "the chord does more if you give it one extra note," and when he asked which note she had shrugged and said she'd found it by accident.

The janitor came down the aisle with a flashlight and a ring of keys, then went back out. Raina leaned over the keys and held down a G, a B, and a D. "This is what you've got," she said. "Plain G."

He stared at the chord. G, B, D. One extra note. In C major, and his piece was in C major, there were only so many notes it could be. He tried adding an E, and it turned into something that belonged in the middle of a piece, not the end. He tried an A, which made the chord comfortable in a way that took all the tension out of it. Then he put an F under his fingers with the other three.

The four notes together, G, B, D and F, did something the plain chord hadn't done. The F leaned. He couldn't describe it better than that; it leaned toward the C the way a person leans toward a door they intend to open. He played bars fifteen and sixteen, and the landing that had felt like a curb now felt like a step down onto solid ground, the whole ending gathering itself and arriving. Raina sat back.

"What is that?" she said. "The chord with the F."

"I don't know the name." He texted Mylie, who answered three minutes later from her house across town: dominant seventh. She added, "In C it's G7, G B D and F, and it pulls hard toward the C chord. I added the F to my G right before the last bar and suddenly it worked." He wrote F into the score in bar fifteen, then copied the whole chord out in the margin of his staff paper so he wouldn't lose it, printing the notes one under another the way Ms. Popal had shown them in September.

He played the sixteen bars from the top. The melody was still his, the same tune he'd carried around for two weeks, but it ended now, and the difference was one note sitting under his left hand. He didn't fully understand why the F should matter more than the E or the A had; he only knew that it did, and that Mylie had found it by accident and he had found it by going through the possibilities one at a time, which felt like two different ways of arriving at the same room. Whether that made his version worth more or less, he couldn't say, and he suspected Ms. Popal would decline to exculpate either method. She cared about the score on the page.

Raina took out her phone and recorded him playing it through once. "Send it to Mylie," she said. "Tell her we found her note."

He nodded and played the last two bars again, just to feel the F lean, and let it go.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Many people prefer $50 now over $100 in a year, yet prefer $100 in six years over $50 in five, a preference reversal called present bias.
story:
Sophia had the fifty dollars in her pocket by second period, folded into quarters so it made a small brick against her thigh. It was the deposit for the summer writing intensive, due to Ms. Bélanger by three o'clock, and Ms. Bélanger had told her, quietly, at the door of the English office: pay now and you keep your spot; pay late and it goes to whoever is next on the list.

The problem was that Layne was selling her concert ticket for exactly fifty dollars, and Layne wanted the money today because the ticket site closed tonight.

"Think of it as an investment in joy," Layne said at lunch, extruding the ticket from the plastic sleeve of her binder with great ceremony, as though it were a diploma. "Two weeks from now. Front mezzanine. Chanelle's already got hers."

Chanelle leaned across the table. "If you don't come we're going without you, and you'll hear about it for the rest of your natural life."

Sophia looked at the ticket. The band's name was printed in a font that looked like something had gone wrong at the press, letters half-dissolved into smoke, and she could already feel the specific ache of missing it, the photos Chanelle would post, the story she wouldn't be inside of. She put her hand in her pocket and touched the folded bill without pulling it out.

"Can I decide after fifth?" she said.

"You can decide now," Layne said, but she slid the ticket back into the binder.

In fifth period, which was free, Sophia went to the library and sat across from Ms. Bélanger, who was marking essays with a green pen and eating almonds from a ziplock bag like some cheerful ascetic who had permitted herself exactly one indulgence. Sophia didn't mention the concert. She asked instead about the intensive itself, and Ms. Bélanger described the guest novelist, the workshop groups, the afternoon on the last day when everyone read aloud on the quad. She said it was the kind of thing that mattered more looking back than it seemed looking forward. She said nothing about money. She sealed the almonds and went back to her essays, and Sophia sat there feeling both steadied and entirely unhelped.

Here is what Sophia had been turning over since October, when Ms. Bélanger had shown her class a small experiment. Ms. Bélanger hadn't explained it; she'd only put the choices on the board and let them vote. Fifty dollars now or a hundred dollars in a year, and almost every hand in the room went up for the fifty. Then a hundred dollars in six years or fifty dollars in five, and the same hands went up for the hundred. Same year of difference. Same people. Sophia had copied it into her notebook and then, because she couldn't leave it alone, gone home and given the choices to her mother, who had done the exact same reversal, and then to Chanelle, who had said, "Obviously, that's just how money works," which wasn't an answer at all.

Sophia had eventually found the name for it in a book in the public library, and she had said it out loud once to Layne in the hallway, just to hear it: "It's called present bias." Layne had shrugged. Now Sophia sat in the library watching Ms. Bélanger's pen move, and the whole thing felt less like a notebook fact and more like a hand she could actually see holding her wrist.

The fifty in her pocket was now. The intensive was a year from now, in the sense that everything that would follow it, the portfolio, the applications, the person she kept claiming she wanted to become, was a year from now or further. And the concert was now, or near enough that her mind was already spending it. She could feel the two of them side by side, the smoke-letters and the quad in June, and she noticed something that made her almost laugh: if Layne had offered her the ticket for fifty dollars to be paid next year, she'd have refused without a flicker. She was patient about next year and impatient about today, patient about the future and reckless about the near edge of it, and there was no good reason the near edge should count for so much except that it was near.

What she still couldn't tell, honestly, was whether the intensive was worth more than one night, or whether she just liked the idea of being the kind of person who chose it. That part stayed uncertain, and she let it stay uncertain, because pretending otherwise was how people made bad choices with confidence.

She took the folded bill out of her pocket and set it on the table.

"For the deposit," she said. "Before I get stupid again."

Ms. Bélanger wrote her a receipt. Then, as Sophia was leaving, she said, "I should tell you, the guest novelist withdrew this morning. We're still running it, but I'd understand if you wanted your money back. You have until three."

Sophia stood with the receipt in her hand. The library was very quiet. Somewhere down the table, a boy highlighted a textbook in yellow, unhurried, as though the afternoon were long and had always been going to be long. She thought about Layne's binder, and the ticket inside it, still for sale, the site closing at midnight.

She went back and sat down across from Ms. Bélanger and laid the receipt on the table between them.

"Keep it," she said.

"And the novelist?"

"I didn't sign up for the novelist. I signed up for June."

Ms. Bélanger looked at her for a second longer than was necessary, then put the receipt in her drawer, where it disappeared with a small sound, like something settling.

"Tell Layne," Chanelle said later, at her locker, "that if you're not coming, I'm selling my ticket too, and going with my sister."

"Tell her yourself," Sophia said. "I'm going home to write."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In the law of many jurisdictions and in consent education, consent to any intimate contact can be withdrawn at any time, even after it was first given.
story:
Kaitlyn had told herself the whole drive over that this was not a big deal, which was how she knew it was a big deal. She parked near the east entrance, checked her reflection in the visor mirror twice, and walked into the mall wearing the confident expression of someone who had practiced it. The plan was simple: meet Coleton by the fountain at four, wander the stores, split a pretzel, and then, if it was going well, drive across town to the outdoor movie screen by the lake. He had texted that he loved the lake plan, twice, with two different emojis.

She found him exactly where he said he'd be, holding two cups from the smoothie kiosk and looking like he'd been holding them for a while. Beside him stood Baby, who supposedly had her own errands, and who was now explaining to Coleton why Kaitlyn's bio notes had to be hidden before anyone else in their grade could monetize them. "You cannot let some random account turn your lab-report jokes into content," Baby was saying. "That's just free labor." Kaitlyn rolled her eyes at her, grateful to have an audience for it, grateful for the noise.

They drifted through the mall the way water drifts along a littoral shelf, in and out, touching everything, buying nothing. Coleton was easy to talk to, easier than he'd been in the group chats. At the science store they stood in front of the saltwater tanks for ten minutes while he argued that clownfish and anemones were the perfect metaphor for a good relationship, some biology thing he'd half remembered. "It's mutualism," Kaitlyn said, surprising herself by knowing it. "Both of them get something out of it. Ms. He would be so proud of you right now." He laughed, and his laugh made her stomach do something complicated, and she decided, in that moment, that the whole afternoon was going perfectly. She decided this again at the pretzel place, and a third time at the photo booth, and by the fourth time she was starting to suspect that deciding a thing repeatedly was not the same as it being true.

The truth was that around five o'clock, somewhere between the photo booth and the exit, Coleton had gone quieter. She noticed it the way you notice weather changing, not all at once. He answered her questions but stopped asking his own. She told herself he was tired from work, then told herself he was nervous, then ran out of stories to tell herself and just walked beside him in the noise of the food court, pretending to look at the pretzel menu again.

Outside, the evening air was warm and the parking lot was doing its slow gold-colored emptying. Coleton had ridden with a coworker and had already agreed, in the texts, to ride with Kaitlyn to the lake. That was the plan. She had the plan printed in her mind like a receipt. When they reached her car, he stopped a few feet short of the door and turned his smoothie cup in his hands.

"Hey, so," he said. "I think I'd rather just say goodnight, if that's okay. It's not the date. Today was really good. I just, I'm kind of done, you know? I want to go home."

Kaitlyn's first instinct, which she would not be proud of later, was to argue. She had said lake. He had said lake, with two emojis. Somewhere in her head a version of events played out where she pointed at that receipt and he got in the car because he had already agreed. But standing there, she heard Baby's voice from a Tuesday lunch last month, the one Ms. He had assigned after the assembly on healthy relationships, Baby chewing a fry and saying it so casually it had almost slipped past her: "The thing nobody tells you is you can say yes and then take it back. Any time. Even after the yes. A yes isn't a contract you're stuck with." At the time Kaitlyn had filed it under things that applied to other people, dramatic people, people in scenarios. Now it applied to a boy with a smoothie four feet from her car door in a parking lot going gold.

"Yeah, of course," she said. "Text me when you're home?" He exhaled like he'd been holding the whole evening in his chest. "Yeah. And Kaitlyn, the date was good. I mean it." He walked toward the bus bay, and she stood by her car and let the strange fact of it settle: that respecting something could feel like losing it and also, underneath, like doing something right.

She drove home with the windows down, past the strip malls, past the soccer fields, and caught herself rebuilding the story, smoothing it into a version where she'd known all along he wanted to leave, where she'd been magnanimous instead of disappointed. She stopped doing it. She didn't know what she'd do next time, or whether there would be a next time, or whether a next time was even what she wanted now that she'd seen the afternoon's real shape. What she knew was smaller and more useful: the yes and the taking it back had both happened, and the world had not ended, and she had not made anyone get in her car.

At a red light her phone buzzed once in the cup holder. "Home. This was the best bad-good first date I've ever had. Rain check on the lake?" She read it twice, then set the phone face down and turned the corner onto her street, where her dad was watering the lawn in his work clothes, and she pulled into the driveway and got out.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
Grandmother's violin had not been out of its case in two years, and the case smelled of dust and lavender, the way everything in the back room did. Rose had found it while looking for a spare lamp, and she had carried it to the kitchen table the way you carry a sleeping animal. That was in June. Now it was August, and Rose could get through the first page of "Ave Maria" without stopping, provided nobody watched her.

She wanted to play it for Grandmother on her birthday, at the end of the month. Grandmother had played it herself, decades ago, in a recital hall in the city, and she still hummed it while washing dishes, slowing down at the same passage every time, the passage Rose could not get past. The problem was concrete: the sheet music, photocopied years ago by Rose's mother, was missing its second page. Rose had searched the whole house. She had called the music shop in town, which did not carry it. She had ordered it online, twice, and both times the wrong arrangement arrived.

Jaeden found her on the porch with the violin, running the last line of the first page over and over. He was in her grade at school, though they had never spoken much, and he was staying with his aunt down the road for the summer. He did not say hello. He listened for a minute, then said, "You keep stopping in the same place."

"There's no next page," Rose said. "I don't know what comes next."

Jaeden held out his hand, and she gave him the violin more out of surprise than decision. He played the whole piece from the place she had stopped, and then, when she asked how, he played it again from the beginning. His aunt had a record of it. He had heard it maybe thirty times.

"But you can't read it," Rose said. He had told her, casually, that he couldn't read notes at all, that he'd started lessons at four and never learned. "How do you even know what key it's in?"

"It's the Suzuki method," he said, as if that settled it. Rose looked it up on her phone while he ate the crackers she'd brought out. Shinichi Suzuki, a Japanese violinist, had developed it. Children learned to play by ear before reading music, the way they learned to speak before reading. She read the sentence twice. It bothered her, in a way she couldn't immediately name, that he could do something she couldn't, and had done it without ever decoding a single symbol.

Inside, Grandmother was reading a pamphlet from the clinic, the new shingles vaccine, and she read a piece of it aloud without looking up: how a tiny amount of the antigen trains the body to recognize the real thing later. Rose set her phone down on the counter. She thought of Jaeden's thirty listenings, of his hands knowing the shape of the music before his eyes ever would. It was the opposite of her own training, and neither was a lesser version of the other. What she wanted now was both.

She found Jaeden on the steps and offered him a trade: she would teach him to read notes, starting from nothing, if he would play "Ave Maria" for her until she could find the second page in her ears. He said it was a deal, and added that it wasn't a deal she could abrogate later just because sight-reading turned out to be boring. Rose told him she wasn't being purely altruistic anyway; she needed the page, and he was the only page available. He said that was the most honest thing anyone had said to him all summer.

They started that evening. He played the missing passage four times, slow, and she put her fingers where his had been, missing, correcting, missing again. When Grandmother drifted past the doorway humming, she hummed the second-page melody, the whole of it, without slowing down, and Rose stopped playing and watched her go. "Did you hear that?" Rose whispered. Jaeden was already reaching for the violin.

"Again," he said. "From the top."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
The line outside the church annex reached the corner of the parking lot before the doors opened at ten. Eva stood behind a folding table of oatmeal and canned peas and counted the people while her hands kept moving, because Mr. Moose, the coordinator, had told her that hands that stop moving cause jams. A man in a delivery jacket took his box and said thanks without meeting her eyes, and the next woman had a stroller with one wheel wrapped in duct tape, and the next was a boy who could not have been older than she was.

She had come because her school required forty hours of service and because her mother had said, more than once, that it would be good for her to see how other people lived. Eva had expected to feel something clear. Instead she felt the specific tiredness of standing on concrete, and a low confusion that the line was this long on a Wednesday, that all these people had somewhere else to be and were here instead.

Asia was at the next table, weighing rice into bags with a scoop. They had chemistry together and had never spoken beyond borrowing pencils, and Eva found this strange now, since Asia was clearly a regular, quick with the clients, familiar with the codes on the intake sheets. During a lull Eva asked her how long the line usually ran. "This is normal," Asia said. "Sometimes worse."

"I thought it'd be mostly, like, weekends. Or a rush at the end of the month."

Asia shook the last of the rice into a bag. "It's not a spike anymore. It's just the way it is." She said her mother read her the numbers off her phone in the spring, that Food Banks Canada's HungerCount counted almost 2.2 million visits in one month, March 2025, and that it was a record for a single month. She said it the way she reported lab results, flat, and went back to the scoop. Eva did the arithmetic in her head twice and both times it came out to a number she couldn't picture, so she stopped trying and stacked cans instead.

A man at the front of the line began arguing with Mr. Moose about the limits on formula, his voice climbing, and Mr. Moose stood obdurate behind the clipboard, repeating that the rules were the rules, until the man took what was offered and left with his shoulders up around his ears. Eva watched Mr. Moose's face afterward. He restacked a shelf that didn't need restacking. She had been taught, at school and at home, that rules existed for reasons, and she still believed it; but she had also just watched a rule land on a person like a dropped stone, and she could not make those two observations lie flat beside each other yet.

Malika arrived at eleven, sent from the high school office with a form for Eva to sign. She looked at the line, looked at Eva, and said, "I thought food banks were for, you know, emergencies." Eva opened her mouth to answer and found she had no sentence ready. "I thought so too," she said finally. "Apparently it's more like a system now." Malika lingered, watching the stroller woman choose between two kinds of pasta, and then left for the bus without signing the form, and Eva signed it for her, a small forgery she decided not to think about.

At the back table a bin of bruised apples had begun to ferment in the heat, and the smell reached Eva in slow waves, sweet and wrong, like cider going over. She carried the bin to the compost and came back with wet hands and a headache starting behind her eyes. Her mother's voice was in her head, the old injunction that charity began at home, and she examined it honestly and found it thinner than it used to be; the home was fine, and the line was not, and the two facts refused to arrange themselves into comfort.

Asia passed her a bottle of water. "You can stop counting them," she said. "It doesn't help."

"I wasn't counting."

"You were counting at ten fifteen. I watched you."

Eva drank the water and looked down the line, which had shortened by maybe a dozen people and still turned the corner. She would come back next Wednesday, she decided, and the Wednesday after, and she would learn the intake codes and the clients' names, and none of that would tell her whether she was helping or only holding the machine together, and she could not tell yet whether those were even different things. She picked up the scoop and turned to the rice.

"Show me how you get it to exactly one kilo," she said.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: 35 senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed.
story:
The town hall smelled of folding chairs and burnt coffee, and Lucas had claimed a seat near the back so he could transcribe the meeting for the school paper without anyone watching him write. His notebook lay open to a page he had titled, with more confidence than he felt, "How Governments Fire Their Leaders." Mr. Menon, his civics teacher, had arranged the press pass, and had said only one thing about it: "Listen for what people assume."
