That morning Lucas had read half a chapter on parliamentary systems, where a prime minister can fall to a vote of no confidence, sometimes overnight. The other half, on impeachment, he had skimmed, and the skimming had left a hole he could feel but not see.

The meeting had been called over the shuttered textile mill, and the hall was fuller than anyone expected. A man in a windbreaker spoke first about federal money, and then a woman stood and said the whole problem was that nobody could be held accountable anymore, not in Washington, not anywhere. "You can vote them out," someone called from the middle rows. "Every four years," the woman said, "if they last that long."

Lucas's pen stopped. He had been thinking of removal as one thing, a procedure, and now he saw it was two things wearing the same word. In a parliament, the head of government stood or fell with the legislature's confidence; in a presidential system, the president was elected separately and could be removed only by impeachment, which took a two-thirds vote of the Senate. He wrote both columns in his notebook and underlined nothing, because he did not yet know which side of the page mattered.

Katarina slid into the seat beside him, coat still buttoned, cold air coming off her. "Are you actually working?" she whispered. "Judith's up front arguing with a councilwoman about the mill." She glanced at his page. "Why two columns?" He told her, quietly, that the woman who'd spoken was really asking a question about design: whether power should be easy to withdraw or hard. Katarina frowned. "Easy. Obviously. If they're terrible, out they go." Lucas said it wasn't obvious, that a system where a bare majority could remove a head of government might just be a system where removal becomes a weapon, and she made a noise that meant she'd heard worse arguments.

Mr. Menon took the microphone during the open floor, and Lucas braced for a lecture. Instead his teacher only put a question to the room: whether anyone believed a bar for removal could be set so high that it stopped meaning anything at all. A man near the stage said yes, absolutely, and cited a case from the 1860s, but the room's attention broke then, because Judith stood up, red-faced, holding a petition, and the meeting tilted toward her.

Afterward, in the lobby, while Lucas copied his notes into something legible, he asked Mr. Menon about the case the man had mentioned. His teacher looked at him for a moment and said, "Look it up yourself. Tonight. Before you write the word 'unremovable.'" He said it kindly, but Lucas felt the rebuke, the small penalty for skimming.

He looked it up at the kitchen table while his mother washed dishes. In 1868 the Senate acquitted President Andrew Johnson by one vote: thirty-five senators voted to convict, one short of the two-thirds needed. He sat with that for a long time, the metronome of the dishwasher filling the silence. One vote. Not one vote to convict, which was what he'd half assumed, but one vote short of conviction, which was the opposite fact and the crucial one. He thought about checking the veracity of the site against a second source and did, out of a habit he'd mocked in class, and the number held. The bar was high, yes, but not impassable; it had very nearly been crossed, at the moment when crossing it would have changed the shape of the government. He remembered Katarina's "obviously" and thought the word had probably never applied to anything.

He texted her the numbers anyway, and her reply came back as three messages: "one vote?" then "that's insane," then "ok maybe not so obvious." He smiled at the screen. In the margin of his notes, next to his two columns, he wrote a question instead of a conclusion: what does it cost a country to make removal hard, and what does it cost to make it easy? He could defend either answer for a paragraph. What he couldn't do yet was say which cost he'd rather pay, and he suspected that was the point of the whole assignment.

The next morning Katarina caught him at his locker, still in her coat. "I told Judith about the vote," she said. "She wants it in your article." She held out her phone, where Judith had typed a headline: ONE VOTE FROM A DIFFERENT COUNTRY. "Too dramatic?" Katarina asked. Lucas read it twice, then took out his pen.

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: Dividing a large batch into shallow containers helps it cool quickly in the fridge, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours.
story:
Gavin's mother left on the six o'clock flight, and the note she'd taped to the fridge ended with the only instruction she hadn't already repeated twice: "Five dinners, or you'll be living on vending machines by Wednesday." He had until Sunday night. It was Friday, past nine, and he was standing in the kitchen with three recipes printed from his phone, a grocery list he'd rewritten twice, and the growing suspicion that cooking for a week was less like cooking and more like logistics.

He texted Royce first, because Royce had done a term of meal prep for wrestling season and would either help or mock him, possibly both. "How do you cook seven meals at once without it going wrong," Gavin typed. The reply came as a message that Royce clearly considered complete: "batch it. sunday. i'll come." Emma, when he asked her the same question at the coffee shop on Saturday, sent him a longer note that he read on his phone while leaning against the kitchen counter, a pot of water already undulating toward a boil behind him. "Dear Gavin," she'd written, refusing to text like a normal person, "the trick isn't the cooking, it's the after. My mom did this when she worked nights. She said the part everyone messes up is the cooling. Don't just shove the hot pot in the fridge and walk away. Think about what the food does after the stove. That's the half nobody plans for. Also buy more salt than you think you need. Emma."

The shopping was its own education. He'd budgeted forty dollars and spent Saturday afternoon pushing a cart through the store with a list segmented by meal, by day, by whether the chicken could do double duty in two of them. At the register he watched the total climb and thought, with a strange adult vertigo, about his economics teacher describing stagflation that spring, prices rising while everything else stayed stubbornly still. His money wasn't stretching. It was contracting. He put back the fancy olive oil and kept the ordinary one, and the cashier, an older woman who had watched him deliberate for a full minute, said, "The cheap one's fine for this, honey. Save the good stuff for when someone's watching."

Sunday, Royce arrived at noon with an apron that said KISS THE COOK and a bag of chips he opened immediately. They cooked in the kitchen in a rhythm Gavin hadn't expected to find so quickly: Royce on rice and the chopping, Gavin on the two pans of chicken and the enormous pot of soup, a tomato-and-lentil thing from his mother's recipe box that filled the whole house with steam. By four-thirty the counter was crowded with finished food, and Gavin stood over the soup pot with a ladle, tired and pleased, ready to clamp the lid on and slide the whole thing into the fridge.

Royce put a hand on the pot's rim. "Dude, no."

"It'll cool in there."

"My coach made us learn this the hard way. One time at the community kitchen we made a giant pot for the shelter, like forty servings, and this woman took one look and made us split it up. Dividing a big batch into shallow containers helps it cool fast, because a deep pot of hot food stays warm in the middle for hours." Royce was already pulling Gavin's mother's glass storage dishes out of the cabinet, the flat ones with the blue lids she used for leftovers. "Whole middle of the pot just sits there hot. That's how stuff goes off."

Gavin hesitated, ladle in hand, because he'd been proud of the pot, of its size, of the week it represented, and some stubborn part of him wanted to keep it whole. But Emma's letter was still open on his phone at the counter, and he'd read the line about the after twice. He found more containers, and one shallow baking dish, and even the pitcher, and they ladled the soup out flat, an inch and a half deep in each, until the pot was empty and the fridge shelf looked like a field of small lakes. He wrote the days on masking tape, Monday through Friday, and stuck one strip on each lid.

Mr. Lin from next door knocked at six with a plate of cut fruit, a habit of his whenever he detected real cooking through the shared wall. "Your mother's away, isn't she," he said, not a question, and Gavin let him in to see the fridge. Mr. Lin bent to the shelf, adjusted one container a quarter inch so the lids sat flat, and straightened again. "She'll be surprised," he said. "She worries. Tell her I saw it."

After Royce left with a container of soup for the road, Gavin stood alone in the kitchen, wiping down the counter, then opening the fridge one more time to touch the nearest container. It was barely warm. He thought about the call he'd make his mother tomorrow, and whether he'd tell her it had gone smoothly or honestly, that he'd nearly ruined the soup with impatience, that he still wasn't sure Wednesday's pasta would reheat without turning to mush. He decided to tell her the true version, minus maybe the part where he'd nearly cried in the grocery store over olive oil. He turned off the kitchen light, and the last thing he saw was the masking tape glowing faintly on the shelf: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, waiting.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
The article was eleven sentences long and Isabella had been on the first one for nine minutes. It came from a German newspaper website, printed off in the school library that morning, and it concerned a plan by the city of Berlin to expropriate large property companies and return the apartments to public hands. Mr. Bear had left the choice of article to her, but he had set a condition: by Thursday she would read a short news piece in German aloud and summarize it, in English, without notes. Eleven sentences. She counted them again, as if the number might shrink.

"Eleven," she said to Usman, who was sitting across the table with his chemistry homework spread like a fan between them.

"Eleven what?"

"Sentences. And every other word starts with a capital letter. Look at this. Die Mieter in Berlin Organisieren... it's not a title. It's a sentence. Why is Organisieren capitalized?"

Usman leaned over. "Typo?"

"There are forty typos on one page?"

Tomas dropped into the third chair with a bag of vending machine pretzels and looked at the paper upside down, which, Isabella thought, was not so different from how she was looking at it right side up. He pointed at the middle of the second paragraph. "That one's a verb, isn't it? Organisieren, like organize."

"So why is it big?"

"It's not," Tomas said. "Look again. Organisieren is lowercase there. The capitalized one earlier, das Organisieren. Different spot."

She looked again. He was right, and it annoyed her how quickly he had seen it. In the headline and the first sentence, the capitals came thick and fast: Stadt, Wohnungen, Mieter. In the body they came slower but still constant, sometimes three in a row, sometimes five words apart. She pulled out a pen and circled every capitalized word that was not at the start of a sentence. In the third paragraph alone she circled fourteen.

Mr. Bear passed the table on his way to the returns cart and paused, but said nothing, which was his way of saying everything. Isabella covered the page with her arm.

"I'm not cheating. I'm finding a pattern."

"Patterns are the whole of language," he said, and kept walking.

She laid the circled words in a column on scrap paper. Stadt. Wohnungen. Mieter. Firmen. Deutschland. Miete. Then, lower down, where the article described how the referendum had gone, Tagen and Stimmen and Eigentum. She said them aloud, haltingly, and Tomas supplied rough English equivalents from somewhere, a grandfather, a semester of German he claimed to have half slept through. City. Apartments. Tenants. Companies. Days. Votes. Property.

"So they're all things," she said.

"Things and names," Usman said. "And also, when you think about it, a German word like Eigentum doesn't just mean property, it means ownership, so you'd capitalize..."

He was starting one of his lectures. Isabella cut him off, because something else was assembling itself in her head and she wanted to hold it there before it dissolved. Every noun. Not just the names, not just Deutschland, but every single noun in the sentence carried its own capital. She flipped back to the first page and reread the opening sentence with this in mind, and the sentence reorganized itself before her eyes: the capitals were not noise, not decoration, they were a map. You could look at a German sentence you barely understood and see at a glance which words were the nouns, which words were carrying the freight. The verbs and little connecting words stayed lowercase, and the solid things stood up in capitals like buildings in a skyline.

"That's why it looked like forty typos," she said. "It isn't mistakes. German capitalizes every noun, not only names. So the capitals are actually helping me."

"That's a generous word for it," Tomas said, mouth full of pretzel.

She worked through the article twice more with the pen, boxing verbs, underlining the capitalized nouns, and slowly the summary built itself in English: Berlin tenants had collected signatures for a referendum to expropriate the big corporate landlords; the vote had passed; the city government was legally unsure whether it could act on it; a court would probably decide. She could feel where her reading was solid and where it was guesswork. The word Durchsatz appeared once and she could not make it mean anything in context; throughput, Tomas said eventually, after scrolling his phone, like how much moves through a system. In a housing article it seemed to mean how many people the market pushes through apartments. She wrote it down with a question mark she did not erase.

Thursday came. The others gathered in the library's corner by the window, Mr. Bear with his coffee, Usman filming on his phone despite being told not to. Isabella read the first sentence aloud, slowly, and her voice caught on one word, Wohnungsgesellschaften, which ran on like a train. She started it over, broke it in what she hoped were the right places, and got through. Then she closed the paper and gave the summary, and it was shorter than she wanted, and it hedged where she wished it didn't. The court part, she said, might be a later court case and not this one; she was honest about that because she could not be anything else.

Mr. Bear asked whether the referendum's backers were sanguine about the outcome. She thought of the photograph that ran with the article, the crowd outside the city hall, and she said she thought they were, but the article had not really said. Some things stayed uncertain even in a language where every noun announced itself.

"Read me the headline again," Mr. Bear said. "Just the headline."

She picked up the paper, and every important word in it stood up in capitals, waiting for her.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: A 2018 study by Erica Boothby and colleagues found a liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company.
story:
Laurence arrived at the football game early enough to regret it, standing at the chain-link fence with forty minutes to kill before Alexanne was supposed to meet her. The bleachers filled in slow tiers behind her, an archipelago of families and clusters of juniors who all seemed to know exactly where to sit. She had changed shirts twice at home and now the second choice, the green one, felt like a costume someone else had picked.

Alexanne found her by the concession stand, holding two hot chocolates even though the evening was barely cold. "I got you one because you looked cold in your Snapchat story," Alexanne said, which was the kind of noticing that had made them friends since tenth grade. "Also I panicked, because this is a date, technically, and dates make me forget how to be a person."

"It's not technically a date. It's a date." Laurence accepted the cup. "I think that's the part I keep trying to problematize, so I don't have to just be nervous."

"That's very you." Alexanne laughed, and then the whistle blew somewhere below them, and they wandered toward the bleachers to find seats where they could see the field and be seen, in case the whole thing went wrong and Laurence needed a quick extraction.

Mr. Khoury was selling raffle tickets at the gate, and he flagged them down as they passed. "Laurence. Alexanne. Buying tickets for the scholarship fund, or loitering with intent?" He had taught her psychology in the spring, the semester she'd actually liked, and when he heard who she was meeting he only said, "Tell him the parking's terrible on this side, so if he's late, it's the parking."

"He knows that already," Laurence said, but the smallness of it, an adult rehearsing excuses on her behalf, steadied her more than the hot chocolate had.

Safa arrived twenty minutes into the second quarter, and the boy, whose name Laurence had repeated to herself all week, arrived four minutes after that, flushed from jogging up the hill. He apologized for being late and blamed the parking, and she said she'd heard it was terrible on this side, and he laughed at that, a real laugh, and they found a spot near Safa where the four of them could sit in a row with their knees bumped toward one another. The game was something she could narrate when conversation stalled, and it stalled often, in the way first conversations do, each silence refilled with commentary about a fumble or the marching band's ragged formation. When the crowd rose for a touchdown she stood too quickly and knocked her cup against his sleeve, and hot chocolate spread in a dark oval across his jacket, and she spent the whole next play blotting it with napkins Safa produced from nowhere while he insisted it was nothing, honestly nothing, he'd been about to take the jacket off anyway.

Afterward, walking toward the parking lot in the loose crowd, Safa fell into step with her while Alexanne and the boy drifted ahead arguing pleasantly about whether the referee had been biased. "You're doing the face," Safa said. "The replay-everything face. You knocked a drink on him, so obviously he hated the whole night."

"He said it was nothing."

"Everything's nothing to you too, when you spill on someone. That's just what people say."

Laurence turned this over for half a block. In Mr. Khoury's class, one Tuesday she hadn't been tired, they had covered a 2018 study by a researcher named Erica Boothby and her colleagues, on something he'd called the liking gap: after a first conversation, people usually underestimate how much the other person liked them and enjoyed their company. She'd written it down then because it sounded like a fact she would someday need, and now, at the edge of the parking lot under the stadium lights, she took it out and held it against the evening like a ruler. He had laughed at the parking joke. He had moved his jacket to the other side, away from her cup, without being asked. He had asked what she was studying, and then a second question about her answer, which people did when they were interested, not when they were counting minutes.

"So maybe he liked it," she said, testing the sentence aloud.

"Maybe," Safa said, "or maybe you're problematizing a jacket stain into evidence."

Both were possible; that was the honest part. She could hold the study in one hand and the spill in the other and still not know, because the gap went both directions, and she had no access to the inside of his head, only to gestures she could read generously or stingily. She decided, provisionally, to read them generously, and to notice that this was a choice she was making, and that it might still be wrong.

At the cars, Alexanne and the boy were still talking, and he turned back before getting into his, and called across the space between them, "Hey, do you text? Like, is that a thing we're doing?"

Safa squeezed her arm once and said nothing at all.

"Yes," Laurence called back. "That's a thing we're doing."

"Good," he said, still standing there with the chocolate stain drying on his sleeve. "Because I had a really good time, and I've been trying to figure out how to say that for two quarters."

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: At the same interest rate, a longer loan term lowers the monthly payment but increases the total interest paid over the life of the loan.
story:
David had been saving since September, taping a printed photograph of the gray hatchback to the inside of his locker so he would see it every time the door swung open. The car belonged to Mr. Sutton, who taught earth science and coached cross country, and who had mentioned one afternoon after practice, while collecting cones in the fading light, that he was selling it. Two thousand dollars, he had said, or David could pay in installments, because he knew what it was to be sixteen with a job at the school store and no bank account worth the name.

The next morning Mr. Sutton handed him a single page, folded in half. David read it at the bench by the gym doors, where the hallway smelled of floor wax and cold rain. The note laid out two options in Mr. Sutton's cramped, careful handwriting. The first was twenty-four months at ninety-five dollars a month. The second was eighty-four months, seven years, at thirty-eight dollars a month, with interest applied either way. Under the second option, at the bottom, was a second figure, larger than the price of the car itself once everything was added up. David read it three times, then folded the page along its old crease and slid it into his backpack, because Emersyn was coming down the hall with a trombone case and a look of someone who wanted to talk.

"You look like you found out your grade," Emersyn said.

"Worse. Arithmetic." He waited until they were outside, under the overhang where the smokers used to gather before the cameras went up, and showed her the page. "Look at this. The payments are smaller if he stretches it out. Thirty-eight instead of ninety-five. That's what I can actually afford, that's barely lunch money. But then the whole thing, all of it together, costs more. A lot more."

Emersyn tilted the paper toward the gray light. "So the longer term costs less every month and more overall."

"Seven years," David said. "I'd be paying for that car until I'm twenty-three. For a car with a hundred and sixty thousand miles on it." He thought of his father, four years ago, standing in the driveway in his work shirt while two men from the finance company expropriated the sedan they had somehow never stopped calling his, the whole thing handled politely, clipboards and everything, his father's hand resting on the hood one last time as if the metal were igneous and still cooling from some eruption David hadn't witnessed. He had been twelve. Nobody had explained any of it. He had gathered, later, in fragments, that the payments had been small and had gone on forever and had finally swallowed the car anyway.

Karis found them there, hood up against the drizzle, holding her own savings ledger, a spiral notebook she kept because she distrusted apps. She listened while David laid it out, and then she said the thing that rearranged the problem in his head. "You know it works both ways, right? Same rate, but time. When I put my paycheck in the credit union, the lady said every month it sits there, the interest gets added, and then the interest earns interest. Time costs you when you owe and pays you when you own." She said it plainly, the way she said most things, and turned her ledger toward him to show the slow, unimpressive climb of forty dollars a month, forty-two, forty-four, the numbers gathering themselves like a small archipelago of islands off a coast, separate at first, then linked.

The twist came at lunch, when Mr. Sutton sat down across from David with his coffee and did not open his thermos. "I did the numbers last night," he said. "The seven-year option. I shouldn't have offered it. It was the kind of deal a dealership offers, and I'd be a poor excuse for a teacher if I made it to a kid on my own team." He tore the page in half, then in half again. "Forty-two months, and you can skip December, because the store closes and I know your hours." He stood, patted David once on the shoulder, and carried his coffee toward the science wing, calling something to the janitor about the leaking window in 114.

David wrote it out that night in his own notebook, two columns, the small payments he could almost not feel and the total that would follow him into his twenties, then the shorter term with its heavier months and its smaller sum, and beside both, in different ink, Karis's ledger copied out, the interest arriving on itself in the dark of the account like something patient. He did not know yet which he would choose, or whether the money he was owed for the season's refereeing would come before the first payment was due. He put his pen down, took the photograph of the gray hatchback off the wall, and taped it inside the notebook's back cover, where he would have to open the pages to see it.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: Many parliamentary systems separate the head of state, such as a monarch or ceremonial president, from the head of government, while in the United States the president is both.
story:
Xavier had claimed the corner table by the window on the second floor of the public library, the one with the wobbly leg that everyone else avoided, and spread his notes across it like a fortification. In three days he would stand in front of his government class and argue that Canada's way of choosing a prime minister made more sense than the American way of choosing a president, except that every time he tried to write the sentence down, some part of it slid away from him, evanescent as the breath-fog he left on the window glass.

"You look like a monk," Heaven said, dropping her backpack on the chair across from him. "That whole thing you're doing, the one lamp and the silence. Asceticism."

"I'm studying."

"You're suffering. There's a difference." She pulled a book toward her, squinting at his diagrams. "Why does this arrow go from the parliament to the prime minister and this other one goes from the voters to the president? Which way is better?"

"That's the problem. I don't know yet. I keep switching sides." He tapped the page. "In a parliamentary system, the party that wins the most seats just picks its leader, and that person becomes the head of government. The legislature can also vote them out if they lose confidence. In the United States, the president is elected separately and serves a fixed term, and removing them takes impeachment, which almost never works."

"So which one do you like?"

"I liked the parliamentary one on Tuesday and the presidential one on Thursday. Ask me tomorrow."

Heaven laughed, and Abigael appeared behind her with a stack of books she was pretending to return, though Xavier could see her library card still tucked in the top volume. She sat down without being asked, which was how she joined most conversations.

"I have a question," she said. "I was helping at the student council mock election yesterday, at the polling station in the gym. A ninth grader came through and saw the poster with all the flags. She pointed at the UK one and asked me why some countries have both a king and a prime minister. Who's actually in charge? I said I'd find out."

Xavier opened his mouth and then closed it, because for once the answer was already on his table. He turned his diagram around so she could see it.

"That's the part I only figured out yesterday," he said. "In many parliamentary systems, the head of state and the head of government are two different people. The head of state is the monarch or a ceremonial president, and the head of government is the prime minister, who actually runs things. But in the United States, the president is both at once. One person does the two jobs."

"Wait." Abigael frowned. "So the king does nothing?"

"He does the state stuff," Xavier said. "The ceremonies. Like if you split the president into a symbol and a manager."

"That's weird."

"It's less weird than it sounds. It's like how Ms. Tesfaye is the head librarian but the shelving system belongs to the whole library board." He heard himself say it and paused, because the comparison had just clarified something he'd been circling for a week. "Actually no, that's a bad example. The point isn't that one is more efficient. The point is what each system makes easy and what it makes hard. Parliamentary systems can remove a prime minister quickly, but they can also remove them for purely political reasons. Presidential systems are stable, but they can be stuck with someone they badly want gone."

Heaven had been quiet, which was unusual enough that both of them looked at her. She was reading his notes.

"You've been trying to pick a winner," she said. "That's why it keeps sliding around. Maybe there isn't one. Maybe you just say both of them trade something for something."

Xavier sat back. The window fog had faded and the streetlights outside were coming on, and the ninth grader's question kept circling in his head, the girl at the polling station with the flags. He picked up his pen.

"So I contextualize it," he said, writing as he talked. "What problem was each system built to solve? If a country wants a national symbol above the political fight, separating the two roles gives it that. If it wants one person directly accountable to the voters, it fuses them." He crossed out his old thesis sentence and wrote a new one underneath, messier but truer: which system fits depends on what a country is afraid of.

"That's not a conclusion," Abigael said.

"It's a considered position. It's just honest about what I can't settle."

Ms. Tesfaye appeared at the table with the closing-hour cart, tapping the lamp. "Five minutes, scholars." Then she paused at his diagram, still turned outward. "Who did the arrow work?"

"Me and a ninth grader I never met," Xavier said.

He copied the diagram into his notebook, drew a small crown beside the ceremonial box and a single star beside the American one, and slid the original across the table to Abigael. "For the girl with the flags," he said. "Tell her the king and the prime minister aren't rivals. They're two halves of a job the United States gave to one person."

Abigael folded the page into her book with the library card, and the three of them carried their things down toward the doors while the shelving lights went dark behind them.

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Ramadan, many Muslims break each day's fast at the sunset meal, iftar, by first eating a date, following the practice of the Prophet Muhammad.
story:
The cemetery gate was still warm from the afternoon when Sophie pushed through it, a paper bag of dates crinkling against her hip. Her grandmother had been buried here in March, under the plane tree near the eastern wall, and every evening since Ramadan began, someone in the family had come to read a sura at the grave before hurrying home before sunset. Tonight that someone was Sophie, and tonight, for the first time, she was also the one responsible for the meal itself.

"You're sure you want both jobs?" her mother had asked that morning, not unkindly, sliding the list of guests across the kitchen table. Uncles who arrived late and complained. Cousins who ate only the fried things. Her father, who had led every iftar since Sophie could remember, now staying late at the hospital where her grandfather had been admitted on Tuesday. Sophie had said yes before she finished reading the list, and had spent the rest of the day wondering whether confidence and readiness were actually the same thing, or whether she had merely confused them.

She knelt at the grave and brushed dry grass from the edge of the stone. Her grandmother had taught her the order of things years ago, in this same cemetery, on the day they buried Sophie's grandfather the first: that you break the fast with a date first, before anything else touches your tongue. "The Prophet did it this way," her grandmother had said, pressing one into Sophie's small palm, "so we do too." Sophie had been seven and had mostly understood it as a rule about dates, the way a child understands most of religion. Now she understood it as a rule about continuity, though she could not have said whether that was more true or just more flattering to her seventeen years.

Her phone showed 7:41. Sunset at 8:06. Twenty-five minutes to walk home, and the lentils still needed finishing, and the recalcitrant oven door that had to be lifted and shoved simultaneously or it would not close. She stood, brushed off her knees, and nearly collided with Ms. Petrov, the neighbour from two doors down, who was carrying a small watering can toward a plot Sophie had never noticed.

"You're the granddaughter," Ms. Petrov said. It wasn't a question. "I've seen you here. Orthodox, on my side, but we water the same ground." She tilted the can over a patch of purple flowers. "What's in the bag? You carry it like it's fragile."

"Dates," Sophie said. "We break the fast with them. At sunset. The meal's called iftar. I'm running it tonight. All of it." Saying it out loud made it slightly more real, and also slightly more alarming, the way signing a form makes a decision official and inescapable at once.

Ms. Petrov nodded slowly, as though Sophie had said something worth more than a passing reply. "My mother ran our feast days," she said. "I never did. I always watched from the kitchen door. It seemed like happenstance, who got asked and who didn't, but of course it wasn't. It was a choice, theirs and mine together." She set the watering can down. "Go on, then. The sun won't wait for either of us."

Sophie walked fast, then faster. At home the kitchen was controlled chaos: her aunt fermenting yogurt in a cloth-covered bowl by the window, cousins arguing over who would fill the water glasses, the oven door proving as stubborn as promised until Sophie lifted and shoved in one decisive motion and it sealed with a satisfying clang. She set the dates in a bowl at the head of the table, counted them twice, and put three extra in her pocket for the uncles who never took just one.

At 8:05 the family gathered. Her father's chair stood empty at the head of the table, and Sophie, after a moment's hesitation, did not move it, did not sit in it either, but stood beside it. The light through the window went copper, then grey. Her little cousin tugged her sleeve. "Now?" he asked. She watched the sky over the rooftops, waiting for the exact edge of it, the way her grandmother had waited, the way the Prophet had waited, and when the last rim of sun slipped below the line of chimneys she picked up a date and held it out to him first.

"Now," Sophie said.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: A 2011 analysis of the Dunedin Study found that children with lower self-control were more likely to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions as adults.
story:
The poster behind Ms. Somsak's desk said DECISIONS TODAY SHAPE TOMORROW in letters the colour of a sunburn, and Hannah decided not to mention that she'd come in about a deposit deadline. Two colleges, one scholarship, and everything due by midnight. Ms. Somsak was on the phone, so Hannah sat in the plastic chair and rehearsed her question, which was really two questions wearing one coat: whether to spend her savings on the faraway school or stay close and keep her job at the rec centre, and whether to tell the supervisor that Lynden had skipped four shifts this month, two of them hers to cover.

While she waited, she picked up the top of a stack of photocopied articles Ms. Somsak kept for the undecided. Most were about financial aid. The third one was from a journal, and Hannah read the abstract the way she read anything free in a waiting room, out of boredom. Then she read it again. A 2011 analysis of something called the Dunedin Study had found that children with lower self-control were more likely, as adults, to have poorer health, less wealth and criminal convictions. She mouthed the words "as adults" without sound, as though they might mean something different spoken quietly.

"That's the one I give to seniors who think senior year doesn't count," Ms. Somsak said, hanging up. "Sorry. Twenty minutes on hold about a transcript. What can I do for you?"

Hannah put the paper down, embarrassed, as if caught reading someone's diary. "Is it real? The study. It sounds like something a gym teacher would invent."

"It's real. New Zealand. They followed people for decades." Ms. Somsak pulled her chair in. "But you didn't come here about New Zealand."

Hannah laid it out: the deposit, the money she'd saved from the rec centre, the midnight deadline, and Lynden, who kept not showing up, leaving her to titrate her patience shift by shift, deciding each time how much of her Saturday to give away without saying anything to anyone. She'd been measuring it out like that for a month. Tonight the supervisor wanted to know why the schedule kept breaking, and Hannah had until close to decide whether the honest answer included his name.

"Four shifts," Ms. Somsak said, not as a question.

"Two were mine to cover. He texted 'family stuff' both times." Hannah found she was still holding the article. "And I read this thing, and now I'm sitting here thinking every skipped shift is a low self-control kid becoming a convicted adult, and that's insane, right? One study can't make me rat on a friend."

Ms. Somsak tilted her hand in the air, a gesture that committed to nothing. "The study says what it says. What you do about Lynden is a different question. Though I notice you haven't decided about the faraway school either, and that one really is due tonight."

On her way past the front office an hour later, deposit form still unsigned, Hannah ran into Lynden himself, sitting on the counter like a gargoyle, waiting for the bus money the secretary kept in a drawer. His sister, he said, had been in the hospital again, the thing with her blood, and their mother worked nights, so somebody had to sit with her, and he hadn't told the supervisor because the supervisor was, in Lynden's word, an autocrat who heard "hospital" as "excuse." He said it lightly, almost effusive about how reasonable the guy was if you never needed anything from him. Hannah looked at the clock above the drawer. Four hours to the deadline, and her phone in her pocket with both futures in it.

Here was what she hadn't expected: the article had made her angrier at him, and the story about his sister had made her less so, and both of those things were still true at once, sitting side by side like the two colleges. She couldn't make them into one feeling. Maybe the study was right that small habits compounded into decades, and maybe Lynden's habit was covering for a family that had no one else, which was its own kind of self-control, the kind no one measured. She didn't know. She was tired of pretending she did.

She walked back to the supervisor's office and knocked on the half-open door. "The schedule's breaking because of things I can't get into," she said, "but it won't break again, and I need my Saturdays back if I'm staying." Then she sat on the step outside, opened the deposit form, and began, slowly, to fill in the first blank.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: The 'file drawer problem', a term coined by psychologist Robert Rosenthal in 1979, describes studies with null results going unpublished, which makes the published record look more positive than the evidence.
story:
The writing club met in a spartan room at the back of the library, six folding chairs and a table too short for everyone, and Ava arrived first so she could claim the seat nearest the outlet. She spread out her photocopies before anyone else came in: two articles on whether morning study sessions improved recall, one from 2011 that found a strong effect, one from 2016 that found almost nothing. Mr. Shevchenko had assigned them a critical review, and he wanted the review to do more than summarize. He wanted them to weigh the articles against each other and take a position. Ava had read each paper three times and still could not say which one she believed.

Stephan dropped into the chair beside her and pulled a granola bar from his jacket. "Yours are the memory ones, right?" He tapped the 2011 paper. "That one's everywhere. My psych teacher assigned it last year."

"That's the problem," Ava said. "Every article I find on this supports the morning effect. Fourteen of them. Not one says anything different."

"So write that the effect is real."

"It might not be." She said it before she had fully decided to, and heard how it sounded, like she was arguing for the sake of arguing. But something had been bothering her since Tuesday, and she was tired of carrying it alone.

Abdallah arrived with his laptop under his arm and his own two articles about bilingual classrooms, and for a while the room filled with the small noises of a club that took itself seriously: pages turning, Mr. Shevchenko writing the due date on the whiteboard, someone's phone buzzing once and being silenced. Ava noticed that Abdallah kept scrolling past one of his sources with a small frown, the way you skip a song you don't want to hear.

"Tuesday," she said suddenly, "I was in the psych building, waiting for my mom. There was a table of old theses being thrown out, and I took one, because the title was about morning recall." She let the pause sit. "Null results. Nothing. The author tested the same thing and found no effect at all. It was never published anywhere."

Stepaan stopped chewing. "How do you know it wasn't published?"

"I searched the title, the author, everything. It exists only as that copy." She had carried the thesis home in her backpack for three days without telling anyone, as if it were contraband, and only now, saying it out loud in the fluorescent light of the club room, did she understand why. The thesis threatened something. Fourteen published articles, all agreeing, and one abandoned manuscript that said otherwise.

"File drawer," Abdallah said quietly, not looking up from his screen. "Rosenthal called it that, in 1979. The file drawer problem. Studies with null results go unpublished, so the published record looks more positive than the evidence actually is." He turned his laptop toward them. On it was his own 2016 article, the one he had kept scrolling past, and beneath it a citation trail that ended nowhere, an unpublished dissertation he could not get past the abstract. "I thought it was just my topic."

The room went still in the way rooms do when several people stop pretending to work. Mr. Shevchenko did not intervene; he was watering the dying plant on the windowsill with the patience of a man who believed in letting arguments ripen on their own.

"So the review isn't really about which article is right," Ava said slowly, watching her two photocopies as if they had changed shape since the meeting began. "It's about what I can claim when I've only ever seen what got printed." She thought of the thesis in her backpack, its cover soft from handling, and of the fourteen agreeing articles, and how a person could read all fourteen and be honestly, thoroughly wrong. She did not want to write that review. She also did not want to write anything less true than what she now suspected.

"Write both positions," Stephan said. "Say the evidence supports the effect, then say the evidence might be a partial record. That's a real position, isn't it?"

"It's more like half of one." She was already writing, though, in the margin of the 2011 paper, in her smallest hand: known unknowns. "I can bring the two ways of thinking together. What's published, and what publishing hides. But I can't tell how big the hiding is. That part stays open."

Abdallah shut his laptop. "Can I see the thesis?"

Ava unzipped her backpack and set it on the table between them, the way you set down a deposition, face up, testimony no one had asked to hear. Stephan reached for the lamp and pulled it closer so the three of them could read the opening page together.
